One strategy passed the initial gate. This page re-tests it against a stricter
standard: whether any future information leaked, whether the results hold up after
costs are raised, whether the parameters were chosen too cleverly, and whether the numbers still make
sense after correction because we have tried many combinations.
done.132:
Signals are recalculated on data truncated at 40 random points. If the signal on the
truncated data differs from the full-data signal, it means future information leaked.
done.372:
The 15 bps cost is the baseline assumption (10 fee + 5 slippage). If Sharpe collapses
at 25 bps, this strategy is fragile under real execution conditions.
done.380: 3. All parameters, not just the winner
done.536:
If only one value is good and the rest are bad, that is a sign of overfit.
A clean spread across several values is more convincing.
done.590: BTC return over the same period
done.628:
Parameters were chosen only from data before the cutoff date, so the numbers here
have never been used to choose anything. This is the test closest to real conditions.
done.696:
If the effect appears only on daily bars but disappears on weekly bars,
it is most likely micro noise, not an economic edge.
done.780:
The universe uses coins that still exist today. Dead coins have no
exchange data, so the results contain survivorship bias and must be read as
an upper bound, not an achievable number.
done.788: 7. Null test with two block lengths
done.864:
Two block lengths are used to ensure the conclusion does not depend on
a single test parameter choice. A p below 0,05 means it is hard to explain with random data.
done.932:
DSR corrects Sharpe because we have tested dozens of parameter combinations.
A value below 0,95 means the claim of edge is not strong enough to be considered certain.
